body: The human brain is an incredibly complex organ, with new estimates placing the number of neurons in asingle human brain as high as 99 billion (Goreily, 2025).  If, like me, you can’t begin to imagine the magnitude of this number, each of us have nearly as many neurons as there are stars in the entire Milky Way (Hurt, 2025).  That’s a pretty astronomical number, right?  And this doesn’t even consider the thousands of synaptic contacts in each neocortical neuron (Drachman, 2005).  In such a complex system, how does the brain decide which neurons wire together, and how can these connections ‘learn’ our experiences?

Let’s start with a bit of background on how synaptic contacts work.  If you’ve ever taken a biology, psychology, or neuroscience course, I’m sure you know that inputs are received by the dendrites and, if they are strong enough, they will be propagated down the axon, where they cause the release of neurotransmitters (Guy-Evans, 2026).  To understand synaptic plasticity, let’s zoom into the synapse and add a bit more detail to what happens when an input reaches the synaptic terminal.
photo1

As a depolarizing current from an action potential moves along the axon, it causes the membrane potential to increase in the immediate area.  This causes structural changes in local sodium and potassium voltage-gated channels, displacing voltage-sensing segments (ex. the S4 paddle) and opening the central pore and allowing each ion to flow in or out of the neuron (Xu et al., 2013).  This creates a positive feedback loop, regenerating the action potential as it flows down the axon.

Let’s take a quick step back.  We said that ions can flow in or out of the neuron – but how do we know which direction an ion will flow?  Neurons use active ion cotransporters like NKCC1 and KCC2 to establish concentration gradients of different ions, especially sodium, potassium, and chloride (Zhang et al., 2021).  We can use the Nernst potential to calculate the ‘reversal potential’ of each ion, or the membrane potential at which the ions will be in equilibrium and have no net flow in or out.  Here, we simplify the leading constants RT / F to 60 and calculate the Nernst potential at room temperature (Flowers, Theopold, and Langley, n.d.).
photo2

Next, let’s estimate the sign of the current flow.  If a physiological current (produced by the neuron) is negative, positive charges are flowing in.  On the other hand, if a physiological current is positive, positive charges are flowing out.  We can use the Hodgkins-Huxley model to find the direction of current flow (Gerstner et al., 2014).
photo3

To estimate current, we find the driving force (Vm - Erev) for the ion we’re examining: if it is negative, the current will also be negative, and will depolarize the cell.  We can ignore Gion (the conductance of the ion-specific channels), as it will always be greater than or equal to 0.  For our purposes, this estimation is enough to determine the sign of the current, and by extension, which direction ions will flow during channel activation.
note1

A quick calculation shows that sodium has a positive reversal potential and will flow in when the channels are opened, while potassium has a reversal potential below the typical resting membrane potential and thus will flow out.  At first glance, these seem to be opposing effects that would cancel out any action potential.  Instead, it causes a net depolarization.  But how can that be?  Different types of ion channels each have very unique characteristics, including the time course.  So, while sodium and potassium do cause opposing effects, the current flowing through sodium channels cause a large depolarization before the potassium channels open fully.  However, after the potassium channels open, the efflux of potassium ions results in a hyperpolarizing current that attenuates the depolarization caused by sodium and brings the membrane back to resting potential.  The sodium channels inactivate soon after the action potential reaches its peak and require a certain amount of time to reactivate, called the refractory period (Benzanilla, Rojas, and Taylor, 1970).
note2

However, something special happens in the synaptic terminal, where there is a third class of voltage-gated ion channels that allows the passage of calcium ions.  When the depolarizing current reaches the synaptic terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels on the membrane open, allowing a rapid influx of calcium ions.  These calcium ions interact with calcium-sensing proteins on primed vesicles, or vesicles bound to the membrane at synaptic release sites by SNARE proteins.  This interaction causes conformational changes in the SNARE and associated proteins, triggering fusion of the vesicles and the subsequent release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft (He et al., 2018).

Let’s look a bit deeper into calcium.  Typical extracellular concentrations of calcium ions are near 1.2 mM, while the intracellular, resting concentrations are around 0.0001 mM (Gleichmann & Mattson, 2011).  This dramatic difference in intracellular and extracellular calcium concentrations doesn’t disappoint – the reversal potential we calculate from the Nernst equation is over 120 mV, almost 200 mV higher than resting potential.  The driving for calcium is extremely high, so when voltage-gated calcium channels open, an overwhelming amount of calcium ions will flow rapidly into the cell.  However, bringing the intracellular calcium levels back to resting concentration is much slower as it requires active transport (rather than simply opening a channel).
Intro to Neurons.note1: If you’re confused about what just happened, think about it this way: the actual ion flow is determined by how easy it is for the ions to pass (conductance) and how much the ions want to pass (the driving force).  In order to find how much the ions want to pass, we need to find how far away the concentrations are from equilibrium, or how far away the Nernst potential is from the resting potential.  To find the Nernst potential, we look at how different the concentrations of ions are on each side of the membrane, or how different the amount of charge is on each side (since each ion carries charge).
Intro to Neurons.note2: Fun fact: the reason that action potentials only travel in one direction (down the axon) is because the sodium channel recovery is slow enough that the action potential cannot move backwards, as the majority of the channels are not ready to be activated again until the action potential has moved further down the axon (Biga et al., n.d.; Olesen et al., 2013).

body: What does this mean for plasticity?  When neurons are stimulated at high frequencies, the active calcium transporters may not be able to remove all of the calcium from the previous action potential before the next action potential reaches the synaptic terminal.  As a result, the concentration of calcium will be higher each time (Sjöstrom, personal communication, 2025).
photo1

Using the shape of a calcium concentration over time curve typical to excitable cells (Senneff & Lowery, 2022), we can predict what the calcium concentration will look like over time at high firing rates.  We can actually calculate the amount of facilitation by relating the exponential growth and decay curves, but let’s focus instead on the theory of what happens in presynaptic mechanisms of synaptic plasticity.

From the graph of calcium concentration over time, we can see that next depolarization and subsequent release of calcium ions builds on the residual calcium in the terminal, increasing overall concentration.  With higher calcium levels, more calcium sensors will be activated, triggering fusion and release in more vesicles.  Overall, the increase in calcium levels in a presynaptic terminal will result in more neurotransmitter being released into the terminal.  The postsynaptic neuron will then receive more neurotransmitter molecules, causing stronger responses over time during high-frequency firing of the presynaptic cell.  This is called short-term facilitation (Stellwagen, personal communication, 2025).

However, the supply of vesicles isn’t infinite.  So, what happens when neurons run out of vesicles?  Each synaptic terminal has a ‘readily releasable pool’ of vesicles, or a group of vesicles that are already packed with neurotransmitter molecules.  During rapid firing, the vesicle pool depletes more quickly than it can be replenished (due to rate-limiting reactions in the neurotransmitter synthesis pathways).  As a result, the amount of neurotransmitter released over time will diminish, resulting in smaller postsynaptic responses during intense firing of the presynaptic cell, or short-term depression (Sjöstrom, personal communication, 2026; Stellwagen, personal communication, 2025).

Again, these two opposite effects, short-term facilitation and short-term depression, seem like they would cancel each other out.  So, why don’t they?  Simply speaking, if the synaptic terminal doesn’t tend to release a lot of vesicles, then rapid firing won’t significantly deplete the readily releasable pool.  As the neuron continues to release vesicles, the effect of residual calcium will prevail, increasing the fraction of vesicles that are released and thus resulting in short-term facilitation (Sjöstrom, personal communication, 2026).  Now, let’s work through the logic behind this phenomenon.

Synapses don’t always release neurotransmitters when the synaptic terminal depolarizes.  Instead, each release site has a characteristic probability of release.  Let’s do a quick thought experiment.  Assume that two synapses have the same size readily releasable pool and they generate new neurotransmitter-filled vesicles at the same rate.  However, one synapse has a high release rate (p = 0.80), while the other synapse has a low release rate (p = 0.20).  What will happen to both readily releasable pools over time when we fire at a high frequency?

Let’s look at the first few times each synapse fires.  We can model the depletion of remaining vesicles over time with an exponential equation n • (1 - p)i, where i is the number of times the neuron fires.  The effect of release probability on the readily releasable pool is obvious with the first two times a neuron fires – when p = 0.80 (80% of the vesicles are released), the readily releasable pool will deplete to 4% of its original size.  On the other hand, the low release probability release site will show a depletion of the readily releasable pool to 64% of its original size.  Of course, in an actual brain, the neuron will replenish a certain fraction of the readily releasable pool before the neuron fires again.  However, we can already see the effect of release probability on the readily releasable pool even with this quick estimate.

When a synaptic release site has a high release probability, the effect of readily releasable pool depletion will predominate, resulting in short-term depression.  However, when a synaptic release site has a low release probability, the effect of residual calcium will predominate as there are enough vesicles left to release, resulting in short-term facilitation.
